warmup.q: Two threads run the store-buffering test from lesson 1 of this track with a VarHandle. Thread A: X.setRelease(p, 1); r1 = (int) Y.getAcquire(p);. Thread B: Y.setRelease(p, 1); r2 = (int) X.getAcquire(p);. Can both r1 and r2 end up 0?
options: No: release plus acquire is everything volatile does
Only on ARM, because x86 never reorders
Only if the fields are long or double
warmup.why: Release keeps earlier accesses before the write, and acquire keeps later accesses after the read. Neither stops a thread's read from overtaking its own earlier write, and that's exactly what x86's store buffer does. Volatile adds one total order over all volatile accesses, which is what forbids both reading 0. The jcstress sample BasicJMM_07_Consensus recorded it in 6.18% of samples with acquire/release and never with volatile.

sections.h: A VarHandle puts the memory mode on each access
sections.html:
volatile puts the memory rules on the field: every read and write of it is a volatile access, whether that access needs the full rules or not. A one-producer queue that only needs its data to arrive in order still pays, on x86, for the store-buffer drain after every volatile write (lesson 3 of this track), millions of times a second. A VarHandle puts the rules on each access instead. VarHandles came in JDK 9 with JEP 193. (A JEP, or JDK Enhancement Proposal, is the public design document for one JDK feature.) A VarHandle is a typed handle to one field or array element, with one method per mode: get and set (plain), getOpaque and setOpaque, getAcquire and setRelease, getVolatile and setVolatile. It also has atomic updates such as compareAndSet, getAndAdd and getAndSet.

Java
final class SettlementSlot {
    private static final VarHandle ITEM;              // 1. one handle per field, static final
    static {
        try {
            ITEM = MethodHandles.lookup()              // 2. a lookup that can see the private field
                    .findVarHandle(SettlementSlot.class, "item", Settlement.class);
        } catch (ReflectiveOperationException e) {
            throw new ExceptionInInitializerError(e);
        }
    }

    private Settlement item;                           // 3. a plain field: the mode goes on each access

    Settlement peek() {
        return (Settlement) ITEM.getAcquire(this);     // 4. receiver first, cast the result
    }
}
Kotlin
class SettlementSlot {
    private var item: Settlement? = null               // 3. a plain field: the mode goes on each access

    fun peek(): Settlement? = ITEM.getAcquire(this) as Settlement?   // 4. receiver first, cast the result

    companion object {
        // 1. one handle per field; 2. looked up inside the class, so it can see the private field
        private val ITEM: VarHandle = MethodHandles.lookup()
            .findVarHandle(SettlementSlot::class.java, "item", Settlement::class.java)
    }
}

Three details make this work.

Keep the handle in a static final field. The JIT treats a static final as a constant, so it can compile ITEM.getAcquire(this) down to one load plus whatever barrier the mode needs. In Kotlin, a private val in the companion object compiles to exactly that field.

The access methods are signature-polymorphic. The compiler records the argument types and the cast on the result as the call's real signature, and the VarHandle checks them when the call runs. Kotlin 2 does the same: the as cast sets the return type. Types that can't be converted fail at runtime, with WrongMethodTypeException or ClassCastException, not at compile time.

The mode at the access wins over the declaration. The Javadoc says a plain get reads a field as plain "even if that field is declared volatile", and warns that mixing modes on one field needs "extreme care". So keep the field plain, and send every access through the handle.

You don't need the boilerplate to use the modes. Since JDK 9, AtomicInteger, AtomicLong and AtomicReference have getPlain, getOpaque, getAcquire, setRelease and friends. The old lazySet (JDK 6) is setRelease under another name. What a VarHandle saves is the extra object: the mode works on a plain field of your own class.

Check yourself: a field is declared volatile, and one hot loop reads it through ITEM.get(this). Is that read volatile? No. The mode at the access wins, so it is a plain read, and the JIT may hoist it out of the loop exactly as it did in lesson 1 of this track.

sections.h: Four modes, from weakest to strongest
sections.html:
The VarHandle Javadoc defines the modes as a ladder. Each one keeps everything below it and adds one promise.

Plain mode (get, set) is an ordinary field access. It's atomic for references and for values of 32 bits or less, and it promises nothing about what other threads see, or when. The JIT may read it once for a whole loop. That was the hang in lesson 1 of this track.

Opaque mode (getOpaque, setOpaque) adds two things. It's atomic for long and double too. And it's coherent for that one variable: the JIT must really perform each read and write, in order, so a thread spinning on it eventually sees a new value. It orders nothing else. Other fields can still appear in any order.

Acquire and release (getAcquire, setRelease) add one-way ordering. Nothing before a release write may move after it. Nothing after an acquire read may move before it. When an acquire read sees the value that a release write stored, the reader also sees everything the writer did before the release. That's the happens-before handoff from lesson 2 of this track, built from one variable.

Volatile mode (getVolatile, setVolatile, or a volatile field) adds a single total order: all threads agree on one order of all volatile accesses. That's what forbids the store-buffering result, where each thread writes its own variable and then reads the other's as 0.

Mode What can still go wrong
plain a loop never sees the new value; a long tears
opaque a reader sees the flag before the data it guards
acquire/release two threads each write, then both read the other's old value
volatile nothing on this list

The jcstress samples show each step. In BasicJMM_04_Progress, a plain spin loop is allowed to hang and an opaque one is not. In BasicJMM_06_Causality, a reader may see the flag without the data with opaque accesses (0.68% of samples on AArch64, 0 on x86_64), and never with release/acquire. In BasicJMM_07_Consensus, acquire/release still lets both threads read 0 (6.18% in the recorded run), and volatile forbids it.

On x86, plain, opaque, acquire and release accesses all compile to ordinary loads and stores; the modes mostly restrain the JIT. Only the volatile write adds an instruction that drains the store buffer. The Try it measures what that buys.

try.title: Store buffering in four modes
steps: Read ModesDemo. It runs the store-buffering test from lesson 1 of this track once per access mode, 262,144 trials each.
Predict, for each mode, whether any trial ends with both threads reading 0.
Run it (Java or Kotlin). Then explain the opaque line: opaque stops the JIT from reordering, so who is reordering?

code.title: ModesDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.jmm.l06; import java.lang.invoke.MethodHandles; import java.lang.invoke.VarHandle; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; import java.util.function.IntConsumer; /** * The store-buffering test from lesson 1, once per VarHandle access mode. Thread A runs * {@code x = 1; r1 = y;} and thread B runs {@code y = 1; r2 = x;}. Count the trials where both read 0. */ public class ModesDemo { static final class Pair { int x, y; } static final VarHandle X, Y; static { try { MethodHandles.Lookup lookup = MethodHandles.lookup(); X = lookup.findVarHandle(Pair.class, "x", int.class); Y = lookup.findVarHandle(Pair.class, "y", int.class); } catch (ReflectiveOperationException e) { throw new ExceptionInInitializerError(e); } } static final int TRIALS = 1 << 18; static final int BATCH = 32; public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { for (int run = 1; run <= 3; run++) { System.out.printf("run %d: both read 0 with plain %,6d | opaque %,6d | release/acquire %,6d | volatile %,d (of %,d)%n", run, plain(), opaque(), releaseAcquire(), volatileMode(), TRIALS); } } static int plain() throws InterruptedException { Pair[] s = pairs(); int[] r1 = new int[TRIALS], r2 = new int[TRIALS]; race(i -> { X.set(s[i], 1); r1[i] = (int) Y.get(s[i]); }, i -> { Y.set(s[i], 1); r2[i] = (int) X.get(s[i]); }); return bothZero(r1, r2); } static int opaque() throws InterruptedException { Pair[] s = pairs(); int[] r1 = new int[TRIALS], r2 = new int[TRIALS]; race(i -> { X.setOpaque(s[i], 1); r1[i] = (int) Y.getOpaque(s[i]); }, i -> { Y.setOpaque(s[i], 1); r2[i] = (int) X.getOpaque(s[i]); }); return bothZero(r1, r2); } static int releaseAcquire() throws InterruptedException { Pair[] s = pairs(); int[] r1 = new int[TRIALS], r2 = new int[TRIALS]; race(i -> { X.setRelease(s[i], 1); r1[i] = (int) Y.getAcquire(s[i]); }, i -> { Y.setRelease(s[i], 1); r2[i] = (int) X.getAcquire(s[i]); }); return bothZero(r1, r2); } static int volatileMode() throws InterruptedException { Pair[] s = pairs(); int[] r1 = new int[TRIALS], r2 = new int[TRIALS]; race(i -> { X.setVolatile(s[i], 1); r1[i] = (int) Y.getVolatile(s[i]); }, i -> { Y.setVolatile(s[i], 1); r2[i] = (int) X.getVolatile(s[i]); }); return bothZero(r1, r2); } static Pair[] pairs() { Pair[] s = new Pair[TRIALS]; for (int i = 0; i < TRIALS; i++) s[i] = new Pair(); return s; } // Runs a(i) and b(i) for every trial on two threads. A small spin barrier every BATCH trials // keeps the two threads on the same trial at about the same moment. static void race(IntConsumer a, IntConsumer b) throws InterruptedException { AtomicInteger doneA = new AtomicInteger(), doneB = new AtomicInteger(); Thread ta = new Thread(() -> runSide(a, doneA, doneB)); Thread tb = new Thread(() -> runSide(b, doneB, doneA)); ta.start(); tb.start(); ta.join(); tb.join(); } static void runSide(IntConsumer side, AtomicInteger mine, AtomicInteger other) { for (int batch = 0; batch < TRIALS / BATCH; batch++) { mine.set(batch); while (other.get() < batch) Thread.onSpinWait(); // wait for the other thread for (int i = batch * BATCH; i < (batch + 1) * BATCH; i++) side.accept(i); } } static int bothZero(int[] r1, int[] r2) { int n = 0; for (int i = 0; i < r1.length; i++) if (r1[i] == 0 && r2[i] == 0) n++; return n; } }

alt.title: ModesDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.jmm.l06 import java.lang.invoke.MethodHandles import java.lang.invoke.VarHandle import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger import java.util.function.IntConsumer import kotlin.concurrent.thread /* * The store-buffering test from lesson 1, once per VarHandle access mode. Thread A runs * `x = 1; r1 = y` and thread B runs `y = 1; r2 = x`. Count the trials where both read 0. */ private class IntPair { var x = 0 var y = 0 companion object { // the lookup runs inside the class, so it may reach the private backing fields x and y val X: VarHandle = MethodHandles.lookup().findVarHandle(IntPair::class.java, "x", Int::class.javaPrimitiveType) val Y: VarHandle = MethodHandles.lookup().findVarHandle(IntPair::class.java, "y", Int::class.javaPrimitiveType) } } private val X = IntPair.X private val Y = IntPair.Y private const val TRIALS = 1 shl 18 private const val BATCH = 32 fun main() { for (run in 1..3) { println("run %d: both read 0 with plain %,6d | opaque %,6d | release/acquire %,6d | volatile %,d (of %,d)" .format(run, plain(), opaque(), releaseAcquire(), volatileMode(), TRIALS)) } } private fun plain(): Int { val s = Array(TRIALS) { IntPair() }; val r1 = IntArray(TRIALS); val r2 = IntArray(TRIALS) race(IntConsumer { i -> X.set(s[i], 1); r1[i] = Y.get(s[i]) as Int }, IntConsumer { i -> Y.set(s[i], 1); r2[i] = X.get(s[i]) as Int }) return bothZero(r1, r2) } private fun opaque(): Int { val s = Array(TRIALS) { IntPair() }; val r1 = IntArray(TRIALS); val r2 = IntArray(TRIALS) race(IntConsumer { i -> X.setOpaque(s[i], 1); r1[i] = Y.getOpaque(s[i]) as Int }, IntConsumer { i -> Y.setOpaque(s[i], 1); r2[i] = X.getOpaque(s[i]) as Int }) return bothZero(r1, r2) } private fun releaseAcquire(): Int { val s = Array(TRIALS) { IntPair() }; val r1 = IntArray(TRIALS); val r2 = IntArray(TRIALS) race(IntConsumer { i -> X.setRelease(s[i], 1); r1[i] = Y.getAcquire(s[i]) as Int }, IntConsumer { i -> Y.setRelease(s[i], 1); r2[i] = X.getAcquire(s[i]) as Int }) return bothZero(r1, r2) } private fun volatileMode(): Int { val s = Array(TRIALS) { IntPair() }; val r1 = IntArray(TRIALS); val r2 = IntArray(TRIALS) race(IntConsumer { i -> X.setVolatile(s[i], 1); r1[i] = Y.getVolatile(s[i]) as Int }, IntConsumer { i -> Y.setVolatile(s[i], 1); r2[i] = X.getVolatile(s[i]) as Int }) return bothZero(r1, r2) } // Runs a(i) and b(i) for every trial on two threads. A small spin barrier every BATCH trials // keeps the two threads on the same trial at about the same moment. private fun race(a: IntConsumer, b: IntConsumer) { val doneA = AtomicInteger() val doneB = AtomicInteger() val ta = thread { runSide(a, doneA, doneB) } val tb = thread { runSide(b, doneB, doneA) } ta.join(); tb.join() } private fun runSide(side: IntConsumer, mine: AtomicInteger, other: AtomicInteger) { for (batch in 0 until TRIALS / BATCH) { mine.set(batch) while (other.get() < batch) Thread.onSpinWait() // wait for the other thread for (i in batch * BATCH until (batch + 1) * BATCH) side.accept(i) } } private fun bothZero(r1: IntArray, r2: IntArray): Int = r1.indices.count { r1[it] == 0 && r2[it] == 0 }

try.expect: Plain, opaque and release/acquire all show trials where both threads read 0: usually tens of thousands, up to about 130,000 here, fewer in a cold first run, and different every time. Volatile shows 0 on every run. Opaque and release/acquire keep the JIT honest, so what you see is the CPU's store buffer: each thread's write is still queued while it reads the other field. Only the volatile write makes HotSpot drain the buffer before the next read.

sections.h: Release/acquire is for handing data to another thread
sections.html:
Release/acquire has one job: handing over data from one thread to another. The writer does plain writes, then one release write. The reader does one acquire read, and if it sees the new value, it reads the data.

Java
// writer thread
report.total = 1_250_000;                         // 1. plain writes of the data
report.count = 42;
READY.setRelease(report, true);                   // 2. release: the data can't move after this

// reader thread
if ((boolean) READY.getAcquire(report)) {         // 3. acquire: nothing below moves above this
    publish(report.total, report.count);          // 4. sees the data, because it saw the release
}
Kotlin
// writer thread
report.total = 1_250_000                          // 1. plain writes of the data
report.count = 42
READY.setRelease(report, true)                    // 2. release: the data can't move after this

// reader thread
if (READY.getAcquire(report) as Boolean) {        // 3. acquire: nothing below moves above this
    publish(report.total, report.count)           // 4. sees the data, because it saw the release
}

Four rules keep it correct.

Pair them on the same variable. A release of ready and an acquire of done give you nothing, just as a volatile write and a volatile read of two different fields gave you nothing in lesson 2 of this track.

The promise only holds when the acquire reads the released value, or a later one. A reader that still sees false learns nothing, which is fine: it tries again later.

Release/acquire doesn't make read-modify-write atomic. When several threads may write, and the first should win, use compareAndSet. The Javadoc gives it volatile semantics: it reads the current value as getVolatile and, if that value is the expected one, writes as setVolatile. Weaker variants exist (compareAndExchangeAcquire, weakCompareAndSetRelease and others). The weak ones may fail even when the value matches, so they belong inside retry loops.

Don't use it for "I write my flag, then check yours". That's the store-buffering shape from the previous section, and it needs volatile, or better a lock or a compareAndSet on one shared variable.

Why bother, when a volatile field does all this? Because the write side is cheaper. On x86, a release write is a plain store, while a volatile write also drains the store buffer. For a queue that hands over millions of messages a second from one producer, that difference shows up in a profile. That's the whole case for this mode.

try.title: Hand over transfers three ways
steps: Read HandoffDemo. One producer hands transfers to one consumer through a one-item slot for three seconds. There are three slots: ordinary field access, opaque, and release/acquire.
Predict for each one: does it keep going, and does the consumer ever see a transfer with the wrong fields?
Run it three times, adding -Pargs=plain, then -Pargs=opaque, then no argument (release/acquire). Try the Kotlin twin too.

code.title: HandoffDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.jmm.l06; import java.lang.invoke.MethodHandles; import java.lang.invoke.VarHandle; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicLong; /** * One producer hands transfers to one consumer through a one-item slot, for three seconds. * The argument picks the slot: plain (ordinary field access), opaque, or release (the default). */ public class HandoffDemo { static final class Transfer { long id; long amountCents; } // plain fields on purpose interface Slot { boolean offer(Transfer t); // producer only: false if the slot is still full Transfer poll(); // consumer only: null if the slot is empty } static class Box { Transfer item; } // null means empty static final VarHandle ITEM; static { try { ITEM = MethodHandles.lookup().findVarHandle(Box.class, "item", Transfer.class); } catch (ReflectiveOperationException e) { throw new ExceptionInInitializerError(e); } } static final class PlainSlot extends Box implements Slot { // what ordinary Java code does public boolean offer(Transfer t) { if (item != null) return false; item = t; return true; } public Transfer poll() { Transfer t = item; if (t != null) item = null; return t; } } static final class OpaqueSlot extends Box implements Slot { public boolean offer(Transfer t) { if (ITEM.getOpaque(this) != null) return false; ITEM.setOpaque(this, t); return true; } public Transfer poll() { Transfer t = (Transfer) ITEM.getOpaque(this); if (t != null) ITEM.setOpaque(this, null); return t; } } static final class ReleaseAcquireSlot extends Box implements Slot { public boolean offer(Transfer t) { if (ITEM.getAcquire(this) != null) return false; ITEM.setRelease(this, t); // release: t's fields were written before this return true; } public Transfer poll() { Transfer t = (Transfer) ITEM.getAcquire(this); // acquire: so the consumer sees them if (t != null) ITEM.setRelease(this, null); return t; } } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { String mode = args.length > 0 ? args[0] : "release"; Slot slot = switch (mode) { case "plain" -> new PlainSlot(); case "opaque" -> new OpaqueSlot(); default -> new ReleaseAcquireSlot(); }; AtomicLong handed = new AtomicLong(); // progress, for main to watch AtomicLong wrong = new AtomicLong(); Thread producer = new Thread(() -> { for (long id = 1; ; id++) { Transfer t = new Transfer(); t.id = id; // 1. fill in the message with plain writes t.amountCents = id * 7; while (!slot.offer(t)) { } // 2. spin until the slot is empty, then hand it over } }); Thread consumer = new Thread(() -> { for (long expected = 1; ; expected++) { Transfer t = slot.poll(); while (t == null) t = slot.poll(); // 3. spin until the slot is full if (t.id != expected || t.amountCents != expected * 7) wrong.incrementAndGet(); handed.set(expected); } }); producer.setDaemon(true); // so the JVM can exit even if they spin forever consumer.setDaemon(true); producer.start(); consumer.start(); long last = -1; for (int tick = 0; tick < 4; tick++) { Thread.sleep(750); long now = handed.get(); if (now == last) { System.out.printf("%s: stuck after %,d handoffs. A spinning thread stopped seeing the slot change.%n", mode, now); return; } last = now; } System.out.printf("%s: %,d transfers handed over in 3 s, %,d with wrong fields%n", mode, handed.get(), wrong.get()); } }

// consumer only: null if the slot is empty } private open class Box { var item: Transfer? = null // null means empty companion object { val ITEM: VarHandle = MethodHandles.lookup().findVarHandle(Box::class.java, "item", Transfer::class.java) } } private class PlainSlot : Box(), Slot { // what ordinary Kotlin code does override fun offer(t: Transfer): Boolean { if (item != null) return false item = t return true } override fun poll(): Transfer? { val t = item if (t != null) item = null return t } } private class OpaqueSlot : Box(), Slot { override fun offer(t: Transfer): Boolean { if (ITEM.getOpaque(this) != null) return false ITEM.setOpaque(this, t) return true } override fun poll(): Transfer? { val t = ITEM.getOpaque(this) as Transfer? if (t != null) ITEM.setOpaque(this, null) return t } } private class ReleaseAcquireSlot : Box(), Slot { override fun offer(t: Transfer): Boolean { if (ITEM.getAcquire(this) != null) return false ITEM.setRelease(this, t) // release: t's fields were written before this return true } override fun poll(): Transfer? { val t = ITEM.getAcquire(this) as Transfer? // acquire: so the consumer sees them if (t != null) ITEM.setRelease(this, null) return t } } fun main(args: Array<String>) { val mode = args.firstOrNull() ?: "release" val slot: Slot = when (mode) { "plain" -> PlainSlot() "opaque" -> OpaqueSlot() else -> ReleaseAcquireSlot() } val handed = AtomicLong() // progress, for main to watch val wrong = AtomicLong() thread(isDaemon = true) { // daemon, so the JVM can exit even if it spins forever var id = 1L while (true) { val t = Transfer() t.id = id // 1. fill in the message with plain writes t.amountCents = id * 7 while (!slot.offer(t)) { } // 2. spin until the slot is empty, then hand it over id++ } } thread(isDaemon = true) { var expected = 1L while (true) { var t = slot.poll() while (t == null) t = slot.poll() // 3. spin until the slot is full if (t.id != expected || t.amountCents != expected * 7) wrong.incrementAndGet() handed.set(expected) expected++ } } var last = -1L repeat(4) { Thread.sleep(750) val now = handed.get() if (now == last) { println("%s: stuck after %,d handoffs. A spinning thread stopped seeing the slot change.".format(mode, now)) return } last = now } println("%s: %,d transfers handed over in 3 s, %,d with wrong fields".format(mode, handed.get(), wrong.get())) }

try.expect: Release/acquire hands over millions of transfers with 0 wrong. Opaque usually does the same on x86, but nothing orders the transfer's fields before the slot write, so on ARM it is allowed to deliver a transfer whose fields are still 0. The plain slot usually gets stuck within a second: once the JIT compiles a spin loop, it may read the field once and never again. In my runs the Java version got stuck every time and the Kotlin version only some of the time. Both are allowed, which is the point: a plain run that works tells you nothing.

sections.h: When you need them, and why only jcstress can test them
sections.html:
Almost never in application code. Prefer, in this order: a java.util.concurrent class (a BlockingQueue for handoffs, ConcurrentHashMap, CompletableFuture); then a volatile field or an Atomic class; then a lock. Reach for VarHandle modes only when three things are true: you're writing a low-level building block, a profiler shows the cost of volatile or of the extra Atomic object matters, and you will test it with jcstress.

That describes the people who write java.util.concurrent itself (FutureTask and ConcurrentLinkedQueue both keep their state behind VarHandles), high-performance queue libraries, and almost nobody writing a Quarkus endpoint. It's also the supported way out of sun.misc.Unsafe. JDK 23 deprecated Unsafe's memory-access methods for removal (JEP 471), and JDK 24 prints a warning the first time code uses them (JEP 498). A library that still uses Unsafe is a library you'll be upgrading soon.

The bigger problem is testing. A JUnit test can't prove any of this. Your test ran on one CPU family, after one JIT warm-up, under one load. A green run says that machine didn't produce the bad outcome that time. The lab's tests check behavior that is deterministic once the code is right; they can't catch a missing release on x86.

jcstress, the OpenJDK concurrency stress harness, is the honest test. You write a @State class, two or more @Actor methods that run against each other, and an @Outcome for each result, marked ACCEPTABLE, ACCEPTABLE_INTERESTING or FORBIDDEN. jcstress runs the actors on fresh state objects many millions of times, in several JVM configurations, and prints how often each outcome happened. A forbidden outcome that appears even once fails the test.

Two habits make its results worth having. Read the outcome table, not just pass or fail: an interesting outcome at 0.01% is a real bug in production. And run it on ARM if you can, on an Apple Silicon laptop or a Graviton instance. x86 never lets one store pass another, so many ordering bugs simply can't show there. The Try it puts your lab slot under jcstress and shows exactly that.

try.title: Put your slot under jcstress
steps:
Optional, and it needs Maven and network access. Finish the lab first. Then create a jcstress project with the archetype command from the jcstress README:

mvn archetype:generate -DinteractiveMode=false -DarchetypeGroupId=org.openjdk.jcstress -DarchetypeArtifactId=jcstress-java-test-archetype -DgroupId=org.sample -DartifactId=test -Dversion=1.0
In test/pom.xml, change <javac.target>1.8</javac.target> to 21. The archetype targets Java 8, and VarHandle needs JDK 9 or later.
Copy Settlement.java and your SettlementSlot.java into test/src/main/java/org/sample/ and change their package line to package org.sample;. Replace ConcurrencyTest.java with the test below.
Run mvn clean verify, then java -jar target/jcstress.jar -t SlotHandoffTest -m quick -v. Read the results table.
Change your slot's setRelease and getAcquire to setOpaque and getOpaque. Predict, rebuild and run again.

code.title: SlotHandoffTest.java
code.html: package org.sample; import org.openjdk.jcstress.annotations.*; import org.openjdk.jcstress.infra.results.J_Result; import static org.openjdk.jcstress.annotations.Expect.*; @JCStressTest @Outcome(id = "-1", expect = ACCEPTABLE, desc = "The slot was still empty") @Outcome(id = "8400", expect = ACCEPTABLE, desc = "Saw the whole settlement") @Outcome(id = "0", expect = FORBIDDEN, desc = "Saw the settlement but not its amount") @State public class SlotHandoffTest { final SettlementSlot slot = new SettlementSlot(); @Actor public void producer() { Settlement s = new Settlement(); s.amountCents = 8400; // a plain write... slot.offer(s); // ...then the release } @Actor public void consumer(J_Result r) { Settlement s = slot.poll(); // the acquire r.r1 = (s == null) ? -1 : s.amountCents; } }

try.expect: jcstress prints a table like the ones in its samples. On an x86_64 machine in quick mode, a run here showed -1 (empty) in about 65% of 199 million samples, 8400 in the other 35%, and 0 (Forbidden) in none: the test is OK. The all-opaque version also showed 0 forbidden samples on x86_64, in about 133 million. That doesn't make it correct. x86 never lets one store pass another; ARM does, and there the opaque slot is allowed to fail. jcstress is the tool that would show it, if you run it on the right machine.

refs.title: jcstress: the OpenJDK concurrency stress tests (README and samples)
JEP 498: Warn upon Use of Memory-Access Methods in sun.misc.Unsafe

analogy: Think of a shared notice board in a busy office. Plain writes are notes you scribble on your own pad and may never pin up. Opaque writes are pinned to the board eventually, and your notes on one topic go up in the order you wrote them, but notes on different topics can go up in any order. A release write is a sealed envelope pinned to the board: everything you wrote before sealing it is inside, and whoever opens it (the acquire) reads all of it. Volatile adds a clerk who stamps every envelope with one office-wide sequence number, so everyone agrees on the order. The analogy breaks on cost: in an office the clerk is slow and the envelope is cheap; on x86 the envelope is free and only the clerk's stamp, the volatile write, costs anything.
world: In a payments service you'll almost never write a VarHandle, but you run code that does. Much of java.util.concurrent is built on them. Where this lesson pays off is in reviews and upgrades. When someone proposes replacing a volatile flag in a Kafka consumer loop with getOpaque to save time, you can say it saves nothing on x86 reads, and ask for a profile and a jcstress test first. When a JDK 24 or later upgrade starts printing warnings about sun.misc.Unsafe memory-access methods, you know the library's fix is a VarHandle (or, for off-heap memory, the foreign memory API), and that the warning comes from the dependency, not your code. And when a test suite "proves" some lock-free code correct on the x86 CI agents, you know to ask what happens on the Graviton nodes.
mistake: The most common mistake is using a weaker mode than the pattern needs, because "acquire/release is what volatile does, only cheaper". It isn't. Release/acquire is enough to hand data from one writer to its readers through one variable. It is not enough for Dekker-style code, where each thread writes its own flag and then reads the other's: both threads can read the old value, on x86 too, and both enter the critical section. If two variables are involved, or several threads write, use volatile, compareAndSet or a lock. And whichever mode you pick, write a jcstress test before you trust it.

compare.title: The same release/acquire handoff with AtomicReference, in Java and Kotlin

java.title: LatestBatch.java
java.html: final class LatestBatch { private final AtomicReference<Batch> latest = new AtomicReference<>(); // writer: build the batch with plain writes, then release it void publish(Batch b) { latest.setRelease(b); } // readers: an acquire read sees the batch's fields as the writer left them Batch current() { return latest.getAcquire(); } // several writers racing to set the first batch: compareAndSet, volatile semantics boolean publishFirst(Batch b) { return latest.compareAndSet(null, b); } }

kotlin.title: LatestBatch.kt
kotlin.html: class LatestBatch { private val latest = AtomicReference<Batch?>(null) // writer: build the batch with plain writes, then release it fun publish(b: Batch) = latest.setRelease(b) // readers: an acquire read sees the batch's fields as the writer left them fun current(): Batch? = latest.getAcquire() // several writers racing to set the first batch: compareAndSet, volatile semantics fun publishFirst(b: Batch): Boolean = latest.compareAndSet(null, b) }

compare.note: Kotlin has no memory-mode syntax of its own on the JVM. @Volatile gives you volatile, and for every other mode you call the same JDK classes as Java. AtomicReference and friends have had getAcquire, setRelease, getOpaque and getPlain since JDK 9, so this is the readable way to use the modes: no lookup, no casts, one extra object per field. VarHandle calls also work from Kotlin, because the Kotlin compiler (2.4 in these labs) treats VarHandle methods as signature-polymorphic and takes the return type from the as cast. Use a VarHandle only when that extra object per instance matters, as it does for nodes in a queue with millions of entries.

worked.title: Choose the weakest mode for a consumer's record counter, then decide whether it's worth it

steps.say: A Kafka consumer thread counts the records it has processed. A metrics scraper reads the count every 15 seconds on another thread. Right now it uses an AtomicLong. Before reading on, list what the reader actually needs.
steps.code: final class ConsumerMetrics { private final AtomicLong processed = new AtomicLong(); void onRecord() { processed.incrementAndGet(); } // consumer thread, once per record long processed() { return processed.get(); } // scrape thread, every 15 s }

alt.html: class ConsumerMetrics { private val processed = AtomicLong() fun onRecord() { processed.incrementAndGet() } // consumer thread, once per record fun processed(): Long = processed.get() // scrape thread, every 15 s }

steps.say: Only one thread writes, so the increment doesn't have to be an atomic read-modify-write; that was the lesson of single-writer fields in lesson 3 of this track. The reader needs a long that isn't torn and that eventually moves. It doesn't read any other data based on the count, so it needs no acquire. That's exactly opaque: atomic for 64 bits, coherent, eventually visible.
The weakest correct version uses the modes AtomicLong already has, with subgoal labels.
steps.code: final class ConsumerMetrics { private final AtomicLong processed = new AtomicLong(); void onRecord() { long next = processed.getPlain() + 1; // 1. the only writer can read its own value plainly processed.setOpaque(next); // 2. opaque: untorn and eventually visible } long processed() { return processed.getOpaque(); // 3. a recent, untorn value; orders nothing else } }

alt.html: class ConsumerMetrics { private val processed = AtomicLong() fun onRecord() { val next = processed.getPlain() + 1 // 1. the only writer can read its own value plainly processed.setOpaque(next) // 2. opaque: untorn and eventually visible } fun processed(): Long = processed.getOpaque() // 3. a recent, untorn value; orders nothing else }

steps.say: Now decide. On x86 this replaces one locked instruction per record with a plain store. At 5,000 records a second you will never see the difference; in a loop doing tens of millions a second, you might. The price is a rule nobody can see in the code: the moment a second thread calls onRecord(), counts are silently lost. Keep incrementAndGet() until a profiler points at it, and if many threads count, use LongAdder instead.

lab.title: A settlement slot and a kill switch with acquire and release
steps: Run the tests once. All seven fail: the TODOs throw, and KillSwitch has no VarHandle yet. Settlement is given and needs no changes.
Write SettlementSlot.offer and poll with the given ITEM handle: an acquire read to look at the slot, and a release write to fill it or empty it.
In KillSwitch, add a private static final VarHandle for the reason field, the same way SettlementSlot does.
Write trip with compareAndSet, and isTripped and reason with acquire reads.
Run the tests until all seven pass, then twice more. Then ask yourself which of these tests would still pass on x86 if offer used setOpaque, and what that means.
hints: VarHandle methods take the receiver first and need a cast on the result: (Settlement) ITEM.getAcquire(this), ITEM.setRelease(this, s).

Why does offer check the slot with an acquire read and not a plain one? A plain read in the producer's spin loop may be read once and never again. The acquire also pairs with the consumer's release of null.
REASON.compareAndSet(this, null, why) returns true only for the caller that found null. It has volatile semantics, so a later acquire read of the reason sees the winner's string.
lab.done: All seven tests in VarHandleModesTest pass, three runs in a row.

drill.title: A release/acquire handoff from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write ReportBox: plain fields total and count, a plain ready flag reached only through a VarHandle, a writer method publish(total, count) and a reader method tryRead() that returns null until the report is ready. Number the four steps. Then compare. Did you pair the release and the acquire on the same field?

answer.html: final class ReportBox { private static final VarHandle READY; static { try { READY = MethodHandles.lookup().findVarHandle(ReportBox.class, "ready", boolean.class); } catch (ReflectiveOperationException e) { throw new ExceptionInInitializerError(e); } } private long total; // plain: carried by the release below private int count; private boolean ready; // plain field, reached only through READY void publish(long total, int count) { // one writer, once this.total = total; // 1. plain writes of the data this.count = count; READY.setRelease(this, true); // 2. release: the data can't move after this } String tryRead() { if (!(boolean) READY.getAcquire(this)) return null; // 3. acquire return count + " payments, " + total + " cents"; // 4. sees the data } }

alt.html: class ReportBox { private var total = 0L // plain: carried by the release below private var count = 0 private var ready = false // plain field, reached only through READY fun publish(total: Long, count: Int) { // one writer, once this.total = total // 1. plain writes of the data this.count = count READY.setRelease(this, true) // 2. release: the data can't move after this } fun tryRead(): String? { if (!(READY.getAcquire(this) as Boolean)) return null // 3. acquire return "$count payments, $total cents" // 4. sees the data } companion object { private val READY: VarHandle = MethodHandles.lookup() .findVarHandle(ReportBox::class.java, "ready", Boolean::class.javaPrimitiveType) } }

recap: A VarHandle (JDK 9, JEP 193) is a static final handle to a plain field, and each call picks its own memory mode.

The modes form a ladder: plain (no promise), opaque (each access happens, untorn, eventually visible), acquire/release (data written before a release is seen after the matching acquire), volatile (plus one total order).
Release/acquire is for handing data from one writer through one variable. It does not forbid the store-buffering result; only volatile does.
compareAndSet has volatile semantics and is the tool when several threads race to write first.
In app code, prefer j.u.c classes, then volatile or Atomic* (which offer the same modes), then locks. VarHandles are for building blocks, after a profiler asks for them.
Only jcstress tests ordering honestly, and an x86 run can't show bugs that ARM allows.

explain.prompt: A teammate wants to replace every volatile field in your payment service with VarHandle acquire/release "because it's faster". Explain what they would gain, what they would risk, and what you'd do instead.
explain.answer: On x86 the reads gain nothing, because a volatile read already compiles to an ordinary load. Only the writes get cheaper, since a release store skips the instruction that drains the store buffer, and in a service that writes these fields a few thousand times a second that saving is invisible. The risk is real: release/acquire is weaker than volatile. It's enough for one writer handing data through one variable, but any code that relies on the single total order, like two flags where each thread writes its own and reads the other's, would break, and our x86 tests might never show it. On top of that, every field gets a lookup, casts and a rule that every access goes through the handle. I'd keep volatile and the Atomic classes, and only consider modes for a specific hot path that a profiler points at, with a jcstress test, ideally run on ARM too.

deeper.html:
The VarHandle Javadoc maps the modes onto the C and C++ memory model, which helps when you read papers or Rust and C++ code: volatile is compatible with memory_order_seq_cst, acquire with memory_order_acquire, and release with memory_order_release. There are also static fence methods, VarHandle.fullFence(), acquireFence() and releaseFence(), documented as the matching atomic_thread_fence calls, plus loadLoadFence() and storeStoreFence(). Fences order a thread's accesses around a point without tying the order to one variable. They're even easier to misuse than modes. The jcstress samples AdvancedJMM_14_SynchronizedAreNotFences and AdvancedJMM_15_VolatilesAreNotFences show that synchronized blocks and volatile accesses don't work as fences either. Their guarantees hold only between threads that take the same lock, or when a volatile read actually sees the volatile write; you can't use them as free-standing barriers.

VarHandles aren't only for fields. MethodHandles.arrayElementVarHandle(String[].class) gives you the modes on array elements, which a volatile array never could, because volatile there applies only to the array reference. MethodHandles.byteArrayViewVarHandle reads and writes an int or a long inside a byte[] with a chosen byte order and a chosen mode.

If you want the model behind the modes in one sitting, Doug Lea's "Using JDK 9 Memory Order Modes" is the short guide to the modes, by the lead author of java.util.concurrent. Aleksey Shipilëv's "Java Memory Model Pragmatics" is the long version.
